lesson.title: Openness and Restructuring: Gorbachev's Gamble to Save the Soviet System
lesson.summary: When Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985, he launched two sweeping reform programs, glasnost and perestroika, hoping to save the Soviet system by opening it up, but the reforms instead exposed how fragile that system had become.
lesson.body:
The Soviet Union that Mikhail Gorbachev inherited in March 1985 was a superpower in visible trouble, its economy stagnant for years and its leadership aging rapidly. Leonid Brezhnev, who had ruled for nearly two decades, died in 1982, and his two immediate successors, Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko, each died after only about a year in office. Gorbachev, at 54, was notably younger than his recent predecessors, and he came to power convinced that the Soviet system needed fundamental change to survive, a conviction rooted in decades of Cold War competition and economic stagnation that traced back to the origins of the Cold War itself in the years after World War II.

Gorbachev's central reforms are known by two Russian words. Perestroika, meaning restructuring, aimed to revive the moribund Soviet economy by introducing limited market mechanisms, allowing some private cooperatives and small businesses, and reducing the rigid central planning that had run the Soviet economy since Stalin's time. Glasnost, meaning openness, relaxed the government's tight control over speech, press, and public debate, allowing Soviet citizens and journalists to criticize government failures, discuss previously taboo parts of Soviet history such as Stalin's purges, and access information that had long been suppressed.

Glasnost's power to expose problems became starkly clear after the Chernobyl nuclear disaster on April 26, 1986, when a reactor at a power plant in Soviet Ukraine exploded and released radioactive material across a wide area. Soviet authorities were initially slow and secretive in responding, in keeping with old habits of concealment, but the scale of the disaster and the new climate of openness eventually forced more honest disclosure than the government would have offered a decade earlier, and the episode became a symbol of the failures glasnost was meant to correct. Gorbachev's government also released prominent political prisoners as part of the new openness, including the physicist and human rights advocate Andrei Sakharov, freed from internal exile in December 1986.

Gorbachev's reforms were meant to strengthen the Soviet system, not destroy it, but they had an effect he had not fully anticipated. Once Soviet citizens and the peoples of Eastern Europe could speak more freely and see the government's failures more clearly, long suppressed nationalist movements and demands for genuine democracy gained strength across the Soviet Union and its satellite states. Gorbachev also signaled that Moscow would no longer use military force to prop up communist governments in Eastern Europe as it had in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968, a shift that opened the door to the dramatic events of 1989 that followed.
